stories.headline: UAE's Barakah Nuclear Power Plant Struck by Drone, Fire Breaks Out
stories.summary:
A fire broke out at the United Arab Emirates' Barakah Nuclear Power Plant on Sunday after a drone strike hit the area, according to reports. Abu Dhabi's state media office did not attribute the strike to any party and urged the public to rely only on verified sources and to avoid spreading rumors about the incident.

The Barakah plant, located in Abu Dhabi emirate, is the Arab world's first operational nuclear power station and a critical piece of the UAE's energy infrastructure. A strike on the facility would represent a significant escalation in the regional conflict stemming from the U.S.-Israel military campaign against Iran, which has already seen Iranian attacks paralyze Qatar's gas exports and disrupt shipping through the Strait of Hormuz.

Details remain limited as authorities have not confirmed the source of the drone or the extent of damage to the facility. The incident underscores the expanding geographic footprint of the Iran conflict, with Gulf state infrastructure now apparently within range of hostile drone operations.

The UAE has maintained a delicate posture during the Iran conflict, and an attack on its nuclear facility — if confirmed as hostile — could significantly alter the regional calculus and draw additional Gulf states more directly into the confrontation.

stories.headline: Thousands March in Montgomery to Defend Black Voting Rights as Redistricting Rollbacks Accelerate
stories.summary:
Thousands of demonstrators rallied Saturday in Montgomery, Alabama — retracing the route of the 1965 Selma-to-Montgomery Voting Rights March — to protest the dismantling of congressional districts that have provided Black political representation. The rally began in Selma and ended at the Alabama State Capitol, where Sen. Cory Booker (D-N.J.) called Montgomery 'sacred soil' and warned that the current generation risked losing hard-won civil rights gains.

Organizers and speakers pointed to a series of Supreme Court decisions that have progressively weakened the Voting Rights Act, culminating in a recent ruling involving Louisiana that critics say cleared the way for stricter voter ID laws, tighter registration rules, and limits on early voting in states with histories of racial discrimination in elections. Veterans of the original Civil Rights Movement expressed alarm at the speed of the rollbacks.

Supporters of the redistricting changes argue that race-neutral mapping criteria produce fairer maps and that the Supreme Court rulings correctly interpret the law. Conservative legal groups contend that majority-minority districts can themselves constitute racial gerrymandering and that the focus should be on individual voting rights rather than group representation.

The rally drew participants from across the country and reflected growing Democratic and civil rights coalition efforts to mobilize voters ahead of midterm elections, framing redistricting fights as a central front in a broader struggle over political representation.

stories.headline: PGA Championship Final Round Set: Unheralded Alex Smalley Enters Sunday as 54-Hole Leader
stories.summary:
Alex Smalley, a 29-year-old PGA Tour journeyman with no prior Tour victories, enters Sunday's final round of the PGA Championship at Aronimink Golf Club holding a two-shot lead — the most unlikely position of his professional career. Smalley, a Duke University alumnus who turned professional in 2019, has made 85 cuts and recorded 15 top-10 finishes in 140 Tour starts but has never won on Tour.

The storyline surrounding Smalley extends beyond the leaderboard. His mother Maria has tracked his detailed tournament statistics — distance to the pin, club selection, wind direction — since his senior year of high school, and has attended virtually every event of his professional career, including this week at Aronimink.

A Smalley victory Sunday would rank among the more surprising major championship wins in recent memory, coming against a field that includes world No. 1 Scottie Scheffler and numerous other top-ranked players. The PGA Championship is the second major of the 2026 golf calendar.

stories.headline: Update: Trump Leaves Beijing with Boeing Deal Claim but No Confirmed Trade Breakthroughs
stories.summary:
President Trump departed Beijing after a two-day summit with Chinese President Xi Jinping, declaring the talks "very successful" and claiming China had agreed to purchase 200 Boeing jets with a potential commitment for an additional 750 planes — Boeing's first major Chinese deal in nearly a decade. Trump also said American farmers would benefit from Chinese purchases of "billions of dollars" in soybeans. Xi called the visit "historic and landmark" and confirmed he will visit the White House in September.

However, no formal trade agreements were announced by either side, and Chinese officials did not confirm the Boeing deal or agricultural purchases. Notably, Trump told reporters aboard Air Force One that he and Xi did not discuss tariffs at all — a surprise given that a tariff truce struck in October is set to expire in November. The White House said both leaders agreed to create a "Board of Trade" to manage the bilateral relationship without reopening tariff negotiations.

The summit was heavy on symbolism: Trump received an honor guard, a state banquet, and an invitation to the exclusive compound where China's Communist Party leaders reside. U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said he expected progress on a mechanism to support future investment, but provided few specifics. Markets fell last week on the lack of concrete outcomes.

The divergence between Trump's bullish public characterization and the absence of Chinese confirmation has raised questions about what, if anything, was actually agreed. Analysts note that even the Boeing figure — if real — would represent a significant de-escalation in bilateral trade tensions that had effectively frozen American aerospace exports to China for years.

stories.headline: Two Convictions for Chinese Espionage in U.S. Coincide with Trump-Xi Summit
stories.summary:
A New York jury found Lu Jianwang, 64, president of a Chinese community association in Manhattan, guilty this week of acting as an unauthorized foreign agent for China after the FBI raided his Chinatown office in 2022 and accused him of operating the first known Chinese overseas police station on U.S. soil. Lu faces up to 30 years in prison. In a separate case, Arcadia, California Mayor Eileen Wang pleaded guilty to posting Chinese government propaganda targeting Chinese American communities on a website at Beijing's direction.

The two convictions came in the same week that President Trump traveled to Beijing for his summit with Xi Jinping — a meeting in which espionage was notably absent from the agenda as both sides focused on trade. Experts say the cases illustrate a pattern of Chinese efforts to suppress dissent and shape narratives among overseas Chinese communities, with at least 100 similar alleged police stations reported across 53 countries.

China has denied the stations are police outposts, with its Ministry of Public Security describing them in 2023 as volunteer centers helping citizens with administrative tasks such as driver's license renewals. A London police investigation into similar facilities concluded no criminal activity had occurred there. The Chinese Embassy in the U.S. did not respond to requests for comment.

Security analysts say the cases reflect a broader and intensifying Chinese influence campaign that combines soft power — funding overseas projects and institutions — with covert operations. "It's part of the same strategic approach, which is to tamp down on dissent and to shape a clear narrative around the PRC, and to do that in bolder ways," said Lauryn Williams of the Center for Strategic and International Studies.

stories.headline: Bulgaria Wins Eurovision 2026 as UK Finishes Last with Single Point
stories.summary:
Bulgaria claimed victory at Eurovision 2026, with Israel finishing second after a close public vote. The competition, held this year in Europe, drew widespread attention for Ukraine's entry, which set a record for the contest's longest-ever sustained note. The UK, represented by musician Sam Battle — known as Look Mum No Computer — finished last for the third time since 2020, receiving one point from juries and zero from the public vote with the synth-pop entry "Eins, Zwei, Drei."

The result renewed debate in Britain about the BBC's approach to the contest. Critics argued the corporation treated Eurovision as a novelty event rather than a serious musical competition, while the broadcaster's defenders noted it took a deliberate creative risk on an unconventional entry. The UK's sole top-10 finish in the past 15 years came in 2022 when Sam Ryder placed second with a polished glam-rock entry widely praised as a genuine competitive effort.

Eurovision draws television audiences of roughly 160 million across Europe and beyond, making the UK's repeated last-place finishes a recurring point of national cultural conversation. Commentators noted that political voting patterns, song quality, and staging all factor into results, and that the UK's track record suggests systemic issues rather than a single bad year.

stories.headline: FIFA Faces Backlash Over Soaring World Cup Ticket Prices Ahead of U.S. Tournament
stories.summary:
FIFA is drawing sharp criticism for ticket prices at the 2026 World Cup, which will be hosted across the United States, Canada, and Mexico beginning in June. The average resale price for the cheapest group-stage tickets stood at $553 as of last week, according to analytics firm TicketData, while the least expensive available ticket for the July 19 final at MetLife Stadium in New Jersey was listed at $7,734. FIFA last week tripled prices for top seats at the final to $33,970, and secondary markets have shown some tickets listed above $45,000.

President Trump said he personally would not pay $1,000 to attend the U.S. opener, and California Attorney General Rob Bonta sent a letter to FIFA seeking answers about potentially misleading ticketing practices — specifically reports that FIFA sold tickets based on seat categories shown on stadium maps and later altered those categorizations before assigning precise seat locations. FIFA President Gianni Infantino defended the pricing, saying that extreme resale prices do not reflect face value and do not necessarily mean anyone will pay them.

Beyond tickets, host cities face significant ancillary costs. New Jersey Transit announced round-trip train fares from Manhattan to MetLife Stadium will be $98 per World Cup game, compared to the usual $13, citing an estimated $48 million cost to run tournament rail service. FIFA's requirement that host cities fund security and transportation has drawn additional scrutiny, though federal FEMA funding is expected to offset some expenses.

The 2026 tournament is the largest in World Cup history, expanded from 32 to 48 teams with 104 matches, and is projected to generate a record $10.9 billion in revenue. Critics argue FIFA's fee structure — collecting 15 percent from both buyer and seller on its official resale marketplace — compounds accessibility concerns for ordinary fans.
